L54: COMPARING CAMERA SENSITIVITY WITH NOISE EQUIVALENT IRRADIANCE
L55: 
L56: Jean-Edouard Communal
L57: 
L58: Raptor Photonics Ltd.
L59: 
L60: ABSTRACT
L61: 
L62: Choosing sensor technology is fundamental in designing
L63: 
L64: cameras for soldiers in the field. It can be difficult to
L65: compare the merits of ca meras using different sensor
L66: 
L67: technologies using only the specifications typically
L68: 
L69: provided by the manufacturers. The Noise Equivalent
L70: 
L71: Irradiance (NEI) provides a normalized and unique
L72: 
L73: parameter allowing a direct comparison. It is also fairly
L74: 
L75: simple to calc ulate from the commercial specifications for a
L76: 
L77: given wavelength and exposure time of interest. We
L78: 
L79: compare the merits between typical CCD, EMCCD, CMOS
L80: 
L81: and InGaAs FPA cameras.
L82: 
L83: Index Terms— CCD, EMCCD, CMOS, InGaAS,
L84: SWIR, NEI, noise, irradiance, night vision, low light vision,
L85: 
L86: fog, rain, haze, dirty battlefield, C spot, beacons / tags,
L87: 
L88: covert tagging, tracking, locating.
L89: 
L90: 1. DESIGN FUNDAMENTALS.
L91: 
L92: In designing cameras for use by soldiers in the field one has
L93: 
L94: many variables to consider. Purpose, functionality and
L95: 
L96: S WaP (size, weight and power) are probably the main
L97: 
L98: factors. Assuming the camera s will be small, lightweight
L99: 
L100: and low power instrument s, the most important factor is
L101: function. There are many uses for cameras in the field
L102: 
L103: including night or low light vision, seeing through fog / rain
L104: 
L105: / haze, dirty battlefield vision, C spot (laser detection) and
L106: 
L107: seeing beacons / tags for covert tagging, tracking, and
L108: 
L109: locating. In addition the quality of image is also a major
L110: 
L111: consideration. Both of these variables require choosing the
L112: 
L113: optimum sensor technology.
L114: 
L115: 2. PERFORMANCE PARAMETERS AND
L116: 
L117: TRADEOFFS
L118: 
L119: Before considering the expense of integrating a camera, the
L120: first step is usually to evaluate how it will perform. The
L121: 
L122: capacity of a camera to detect light is determined by the
L123: 
L124: fo llowing parameters:
L125: 
L126: • Quantum efficiency, the probability for a photon of a
L127: 
L128: given wavelength to produce a pair electron/hole
L129: 
L130: • Pixel size
L131: 
L132: • Full well capacity in electrons
L133: 
L134: • Exposure time or frame rate
L135: 
L136: • Readout noise per pixel
L137: 
L138: • Dark current per pixel per second
L139: 
L140: Essentially, on one hand, the higher the quantum
L141: 
L142: efficiency, the larger the pixel size, the longer the exposure
L143: time, and the bigger the pixel well depth, the more signal
L144: 
L145: can be gathered.
L146: 
L147: On the other hand, the lower the readout and dark
L148: 
L149: current n oise, then the smaller the detection threshold will
L150: 
L151: be. Finally, the dynamic range within a single exposure will
L152: 
L153: depend on the pixel full well capacity and detection
L154: 
L155: threshold.
L156: 
L157: In theory, an ideal detector would be able to count
L158: 
L159: the exact position and timi ng of every single photon to offer
L160: 
L161: perfect image quality. In practice, one must balance
L162: sometimes conflicting parameters varying for different
L163: 
L164: sensor types:
L165: 
L166: • Quantum efficiency, suffers no tradeoffs. The higher it
L167: 
L168: is over the larger spectral range the bet ter.
L169: 
L170: • Pixel size and full well capacity; smaller pixel result in
L171: 
L172: higher spatial resolution at the expense of sensitivity and
L173: 
L174: full well capacity.
L175: 
L176: • Exposure time and frame rate are linked to the readout
L177: 
L178: noise and dark current. Higher frame rate is desirable to
L179: 
L180: have a high temporal resolution; however, with high
L181: frame rate readout noise can increase. Similarly, if
L182: 
L183: temporal resolution is irrelevant, then long exposure
L184: 
L185: time s are desirable, but in this case, the dark current will
L186: 
L187: increase correspondingly.
L188: 
L189: Each application has its own set of compromises, f or
L190: 
L191: example for hyper spectral imaging the camera
L192: 
L193: characteristics translates as follows:
L194: 
L195: • Quantum efficiency combines to the grating efficiency
L196: 
L197: of the spectrometer to give a total spectral range and
L198: 
L199: efficiency of the instrument.
L200: • Pixel size, translates into spectral resolution according to
L201: 
L202: the spectral dispersion.
L203: 
L204: • Exposure time or frame rate, translate into spatial
L205: 
L206: resolution according to the scanning speed.
L207: 
L208: The choice of a suitable camera for hyper spectral
L209: 
L210: imaging is therefore often driven mostly by these three
L211: 
L212: parameters.
L213: 
L214: 3. SENSOR TECHNOLOGIES
L215: 
L216: CCD, EMCCD and CMOS are all silicon based
L217: 
L218: detectors, as such are typically sensitive in the UV, visible
L219: 
L220: and near infra-red areas of the spectrum. SWIR cameras are
L221: InGaAs focal plan arrays which as their name suggest are
L222: 
L223: sensitive in the Short Wave Infra-Red area of the spectrum.
L224: 
L225: Furthermore, each sensor technology has its own
L226: 
L227: particularities:
L228: 
L229: • On a CCD, all pixels are read through one A/D output
L230: 
L231: and the readout no ise increases with frame rate but can
L232: 
L233: be reduced by binning. Sensitivity, speed and spatial
L234: 
L235: resolution are linked and subject to compromises and
L236: 
L237: tradeoffs.
L238: 
L239: • On an EMCCD, the readout noise can be compensated
L240: by the electron multiplication gain before the A/D
L241: 
L242: output. This makes EMCCD the most sensitive silicon
L243: 
L244: based device and removes the link between sensitivity,
L245: 
L246: speed and sp atial resolution. U nfortunately, very few
L247: 
L248: EMCCD chips are available on the market.
L249: 
L250: • With a CMOS, all pixels can be read simultaneousl y
L251: 
L252: since each has its own A/D converter. This also removes
L253: 
L254: the link between sensitivity, speed and spatial resolution.
L255: 
L256: However, each pixel’s A/D has slightly different offset,
L257: gain, and dark current characteristics which require a
L258: 
L259: non-uniformity correction to emulate the image quality
L260: 
L261: of a single output device. In addition, binning won’t
L262: 
L263: reduce the readout noise.
L264:

L445: 4. IRRADIANCE, ONE NORMALIZED VALUE
L446: 
L447: With so many parameters it can be difficult to
L448: 
L449: estimate which camera to select in order to o btain the best
L450: 
L451: possible performances for a given application. A few basic
L452: 
L453: questions regarding the spectral range, spatial and temporal
L454: 
L455: resolution required can already help t o narrow down the
L456: 
L457: choice. For example, t he choice of a suitable camera for
L458: 
L459: hyper spectral imaging is therefore often driven mostly by
L460: these three parameters, QE, pixel size and exposure time.
L461: 
L462: However, it would be useful to reduce all these parameters
L463: 
L464: to a single one.
L465: 
L466: Noise Equivalent Power (NEP) is the minimum
L467: 
L468: power that can be detected, measured in watts. I t doesn’t
L469: 
L470: take into account the pixel surface area. It is usually used
L471: 
L472: for photo detectors and normalized for one hertz output
L473: 
L474: bandwidth or half a second integration time [1]. As such it
L475: 
L476: is not a convenient parameter to compare cameras with
L477: widely different pixel size and covering a range or exposure
L478: 
L479: time. The lower the NEP is, the higher the sensitivity.
L480: 
L481: Specific Detectivity (D*): is the reciprocal of the
L482: 
L483: NEP normalized over the square root of the photosensitive
L484: 
L485: area. It is expressed in cm√Hz/W or Jones [2][3], unlike the
L486: 
L487: NEP the higher the specific detectivity is, the higher the
L488: 
L489: sensitivity. However, it still doesn’t reflect the wide range
L490: 
L491: of possible exposure times.
L492: 
L493: Irradiance is the power of electromagnetic
L494: radiation per unit area (radiative flux) incident on a surface
L495: 
L496: its SI unit is watts per square meter (W/m 2). The Noise
L497: 
L498: Equivalent Irradiance (NEI) is the light flux density
L499: 
L500: required to be equal to the noise of the camera. NEI is
L501: 
L502: usually expressed in W/cm 2 or in Photons/(cm 2∙s)[4].
L503: 
L504: The benefit of NEI is that it offers a single
L505: 
L506: normalized quantity representing the sensitivity which can
L507: 
L508: be calculated from the specifications provided by the
L509: 
L510: manufacturer. The lower the NEI is, the higher the
L511: sensitivity will be.

L867: 6. CONCLUSION
L868: 
L869: Noise Equivalent Irradiance allows to precisely
L870: 
L871: evaluate the se nsitivity of wildly different cameras and to
L872: 
L873: rank them for a given exposure time and wavelength. In the
L874: 
L875: visible at short exposure time, EMCCD is the most sensitive
L876: 
L877: technology followed by CCD and then CMOS. In the NIR
L878: 
L879: InGaAs cameras have the edge over CMOS and CCD while
L880: in the SWIR, InGaAs is still the only existing possibility.
L881: 
L882: Allowing for trade-offs in sensor performance and choosing
L883: 
L884: the optimum sensor for the application is only the
L885: 
L886: beginning. Defining camera performance, functionality and
L887: 
L888: building it t o meet SWaP requirements then leads to
L889: 
L890: designing a camera that drives the best performance from
L891: 
L892: the sensor.

Driggers L935:   * cite14†Eytan Pollak L936:   * cite15†Robert Grimming L937:   * cite16†Orges Furxhi L938: Airborne target detection in the infrared has been classically known as infrared search and track or IRST. From a military point of view, it can be described as target detection at long ranges where the target image is subpixel in size. Here, the target is “unresolved.” It can also describe the detection of aircraft near the observer using distributed apertures in a spherical detection field. From a commercial point of view, an important application is drone detection near live airport operations.
L939: As drones become more common, the dual-use functionality of IRST systems is expanding. Technology improvements for IRST systems include the wide proliferation of infrared staring focal planes. New readout integrated circuits allow for time-delay-integration of large format detectors. Stare-step sensors in the future appear to be as common as gimbal-scanned thermal imagers. Detection probability analysis and IRST sensor design is different than targeting system design.
L940: We provide a tutorial here on IRST system calculations as well as discussions on broadband versus spectral calculations and new technology considerations.

L951:   * cite18†Erving Ximendes L952:   * cite19†Antonio Benayas L953:   * cite20†Daniel Jaque L954:   * cite21†Riccardo Marin L955: The exciting advancements that we are currently witnessing in terms of novel materials and synthesis approaches are leading to the development of colloidal nanoparticles (NPs) with increasingly greater tunable properties. We have now reached a point where it is possible to synthesize colloidal NPs with functionalities tailored to specific societal demands. The impact of this new wave of colloidal NPs has been especially important in the field of biomedicine.
L956: In that vein, luminescent NPs with improved brightness and near-infrared working capabilities have turned out to be optimal optical probes that are capable of fast and high-resolution in vivo imaging. However, luminescent NPs have thus far only reached a limited portion of their potential. Although we believe that the best is yet to come, the future might not be as bright as some of us think (and have hoped!).
